# Introduction

The development of foundation models in natural language processing has brought forth models capable of handling a myriad of tasks, from understanding and developping code, poetry, law, research papers equally well. Naturally, we have developped an interest in creating models working on other forms of data with the same capibilities. In this paper we look specifically at the domain of Time Series data. It is generally difficult to work with Time Series data as the observations are often highly-correlated, following speicific sequential, periodic and random patterns. Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) are a rising class of models which promise to deliver predictive and classification power with little to no fine-tuning necessary.

We wonder how do these "generalist" TSFM models, pre-trained with a variety of different domains, perform compared to "specialist" models performed on the specific domain of application. Furthermore, we investigate the geometry of the zero-shot embeddings and if they different based on the data being classified. 

Standard evaluation methods often rely on Logistic Regression. While this is often an effective method for classifying linearly seperable features, it assumes that the previous architecture linearizes the input data. In many domains this assumption might fail, especially in the presence of low signal to noise ratio such as in finance or acoustic processing. This false assumption may lead to false-negatives in which a model's embeddings might be estimated to contain low amounts of information when in reality it may contain rich, non-linear information.

In this paper we investigate the zero-shot, cross domain capabilities of these models in four different subjects. We look at financial, acoustic, biological and physics data from which we extract embeddings and finally apply a suite of classification heads including logistic regression, nearest centroid, k-Nearest Neighbours and a Multi-Layer Perceptron. These allowing us to diagnose the topology of the feature space generated by our models using a variety of classification regimes.

# Data
PTB-XL  is a large publicly available electrocardiography dataset [1],[2]. The dataset contains 21799 ECG 10 second readings using 12 leads from 18869 patients. The data has been expert annotated, conforming to the SCP-ECG standard. Included annotations are "NORM" (Normal ECG), "MI" (Myocardial Infarction), "STTC" (ST/T Change), "CD" (Conduction Disturbance), and "HYP" (Hypertrophy). We have also added a "OTHER" annotation for observations that were not given an annotation. The ECG recordings were recorded at a frequency of 500 Hz and downsampled to 100Hz for processing purposes. 

ESC-50 [4] is a dataset containing 2000 environmental audio recordings. The recordings are uniformly sampled at 44.1kHz with a fixed length of 5 seconds. Each recording is organized into one of 50 semantic classes, with 40 examples per class. The available classes can be categorized as animals, natural soundscapes, water sounds, human non-speech sounds, interior/domestic sounds, exterior/urban sounds [4]. The data is pre aranged by the author into 5 folds for cross validation. We reserve one of these splits to be our testing dataset, using the remaining 4 splits as testing data. This ensures balanced training and testing sets.

The S&P 500 (Standard and Poor's 500) is an index fund comprised of the 500 largest stocks. Our dataset is generated from the daily returns of each constituent stock of the index, from January 1st 2000 to November 1st 2025. It has been sourced through the Yahoo Finance API [5] by usage of the yfinance python package. To pre-process the data we adapt the methodology put forward in [6]. We do so by creating windows of 500 days, reserving the first 349 days of the window for our training set and the last 150 days for our testing set. We have split the data in this manner to ensure there is no data leakage, adopting purging (no overlap between training and testing sets) and embargo (removing any observation directly following a training set) methods from [7]. Financial literature suggests that forecasting based on classifying the direction of the return generally performs better than level estimation [8]. To this end, we set the input variables of our models to be composed of the returns from sliding window of 80 days (approximately 3 trading months) with the output variable set as 1 or 0 if the following day's return is above or below the window's median return respectively.

The StarEmbed dataset is a multi-band light curve dataset designed to benchmark astronomical and general TSFMs on astronomical time series data [9]. The dataset is composed of light curves selected from release 23 (DR23) of the ZTF astronomical survey [10]. Star class labels have been expertly labeled in the Catalina Surveys Periodic Variable Star Catalog (CSPVS) [11].

The dataset is split into training, validation and testing datasets. Time series for green and red light curves are given, along with time stamps formatted in Modified Julian Dates (MJD), and a string identifying the class of the star. Several other variables are included but will not be used for our analysis. 

The stars were first pre-classified using multivariate kernel density estimation [12], followed by a classification done by visual inspection to asses their final class [11]. In total there are 6 different star classes present in the dataset:  "CVn", "EW", "EA", "LPV", "RRab", "RRc", "RRd", and "RS". All classes are present in approximately equal proportion in all three splits, however, some classes  have many fewer observations than others, for example, LPV and EW classes which contain 360 and 27075 observations respectively [11].

# Models

## General Models
Moirai is a forecasting time series model designed to perform across domains [13]. It utilizes multiple patch size projection layers, enabling it to treat data across temporal patterns and an Any-variate Attention mechanism, leveraging Rotary Position Embeddings allowing it to treat multivariate data seamlessly. Furthermore the model addresses the issue of probabilistic forecasting by employing a mixture of parametric distributions, leading to a model which can be evaluated using any metric.

TimesFM is a model developped by Google Research [14], employing a Decoder-Only paradigm. Drawing inspiration from Large Language Models, TimesFM follows the same stratgy and treats prediction as a next-token prediction task. TimesFM processes non-overlapping patches of the series into tokens with a Multi-Layer Perceptron, using a Transformer architecture to autoregressively predict following patches. A distinguishing feature of TimesFM is the data used for its pretraining. It has been trained on a massive mixture of 100 billion time points, composed of both real-world data (Google Trends, Wikipedia Pageviews) and synthetic data, generated through statistical models and physical simulations.

## Domain Specific Models

While generalist models aim for universality, ASTROMER [15] demonstrates the power of domain-focused pre-training. It is a self-supervised, Transformer-based encoder-decoder designed specifically for astronomical light curve data, representing the brightness of celestial objects. ASTROMER has been developped to specifically handle the irregular sampling inherent to telescopic observation (e.g., gaps due to daylight or weather).

Representing domain-specific foundation models in healthcare, ECGFounder [16] is a large-scale encoder designed for electrocardiogram (ECG) analysis. Trained on a massive corpus of over 10 million 12-lead ECG recordings, it learns to identify 150 distinct cardiac abnormalities. ECGFounder employs a RegNet (ResNet-based) backbone optimized for capturing the precise morphological features of cardiac cycles (such as QRS complex width and ST-segment elevation). 

Wav2Vec 2.0 [17] is a model developed by Meta AI, employing a dual-stage archtitecture. It first employs a multi-layer Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to process raw waveforms and extract latent feature representations, followed by a context network which follows the usual Transformer architecture. Wav2Vec 2.0's key contribution is a Contrastive Learning objective combined with Product Quantization. The model learns to predict from discretized "codebook" entries of masked temporal steps, effectively inventing its own latent glossary of acoustic units from raw audio. This architecture allows it to capture complex frequency-domain dependencies and local temporal structures inherent to sound.

Fincast is a domain specific foundation model tailed for time series forecasting. It has been trained exclusively on large-scale financial data, encompassing diverse asset classes (equities, forex, commodities) and frequencies. The model uses input tokenization, followed by Causal Attention and sparse Mixture of Experts (MOE) blocks and finally a Decoder. FinCast aims to capture domain-specific latent dynamics like volatility clustering and regime changes that generic models may fail to prioritize.

## Baseline Embeddings

A custom embedding has been generated for each dataset, computing various statistical features in both time and frequency domain. These embeddings serve as a baseline for the other models, demonstrating the explanability of light-weight statistical methods compared to the much more computationally expensive and pre-trained methods.

Finally we include random embeddings, which are constructed by generating 512 Uniform(0,1) random variables. This baseline will allow us to confirm that other methods are generating useful information, ensuring that our lightweight classifying heads are not doing the heavy lifting.
